newsitem.title: UK: Littlewoods profits down as Lottery hits pools.
newsitem.headline: Littlewoods profits down as Lottery hits pools.

text.p: Family-owned retail and betting group Littlewoods, Britain's largest private company, on Thursday reported a 24 percent drop in first half profits and blamed the National Lottery for a 30 percent drop in sales at its football pools business.
Pretax profits fell in the first half to 12.5 million pounds ($19.57 million) from 16.5 million, but last year's figure included a one-off profit of 10.2 million pounds from property disposals.
Group sales fell five percent to 995 million pounds, but turnover from its leisure business, including football pools, was down almost 30 percent to 245 million.
Retail operations, -- Littlewoods stores, mail order and Index shops and catalogues, returned to profit of 4.1 million pounds after a 4.1 million loss a year ago.
The group, still owned by the secretive Moores family who founded the company, is striving to find a way forward as its mixed bag of businesses face increasingly tough competition.

Last year it was the subject of two billion pound-plus takeover bids, one from a former chief executive Barry Dale, the other from a consortium which included N Brown the mail order company and Iceland stores. The Moores family rejected the offers.
Chairman James Ross, a former chief executive of Cable & Wireless appointed in a management shake-up in April, said the results showed the benefits of efforts to improve performance and efficiency.
Ross called on the British government to create a level playing field for Littlewoods' football pools business to compete with the National Lottery

He told Reuters in a telephone interview the Lottery had advantages on tax and enjoyed effective free advertising via a weekly television show where winning numbers are announced. In contrast, Littlewoods faced a higher tax rate as well as restrictions covering advertising, locations for paying out winnings and rolling over prize money, he said.
"So we think, as the footballers would like to say, not exactly a level playing field."
The group has had to slash costs and cut jobs to survive the impact of the Lottery, which was launched in November 1994.
This year it re-launched its football pools at the start of the 1996/97 soccer season and is spending six million pounds on advertising.
He would not be drawn on speculation about the group's plans for its Littlewoods mail order business, the biggest retail division, but recognised that this sector was ripe for consolidation.

"We regard our home shopping as one of our core businesses...Yes I think there has been talk about consolidation in the industry and I think that is likely." But he said the company had no news on that issue at present. ($1=.6388 Pound)
